title: Mahatma Gandhi and the Salt Satyagraha at Dandi: A Pinch of Salt That Shook an Empire (1930)
summary: On April 6, 1930, after walking 240 miles to the Arabian Sea at Dandi, Mahatma Gandhi picked up a handful of natural salt, shattering the British monopoly and igniting nationwide civil disobedience.
keywords: Historical Dialogue 166: நேருவும் “பணம் அல்லது உயிர்” என்ற கேரள அரசியல் விமர்சனமும்
full_text:
Between March 12 and April 6, 1930, Mahatma Gandhi led seventy-eight ashram companions on a 240-mile foot march from Sabarmati to the coastal village of Dandi on the Arabian Sea.

The British colonial state had established a draconian statutory monopoly over salt, imposing a regressive tax on an indispensable dietary necessity that fell most heavily upon the poorest peasants. In London and New Delhi, officials initially scoffed. Viceroy Lord Irwin wrote dismissively to London that the idea of toppling an empire by boiling seawater was laughable.

Yet as Gandhi marched through hundreds of villages, international journalists documented the swelling movement. On the morning of April 6, after bathing in the ocean waves, Gandhi walked across the salt flats, bent down, and picked up a small lump of crude, unrefined natural salt.

Holding it aloft in his palm before thousands of onlookers, Gandhi proclaimed:
"With this pinch of salt, I am shaking the foundations of the British Empire! A government that taxes the very gifts of nature and punishes the poor for harvesting salt has surrendered its moral right to govern. Let every village in India manufacture salt and defy this unjust law through non-violent resistance!"

Gandhi's symbolic act electrified the nation. Across four thousand miles of Indian coastline, millions harvested illegal salt, picketed government depots, and courted mass arrest with serene discipline. A single handful of salt stripped the colonial regime of its moral authority in the eyes of the world.
